headline: Stop copying prompts. Learn to write them.
intro: A copy-pasted prompt solves today's task and leaves you helpless the moment the situation is slightly different, a different client, a different tool, a different day. Learn the anatomy of a prompt that actually works and you can write the exact right one, from a blank page, for anything a remote career throws at you.
creed: A prompt library makes you dependent on someone else's imagination. Learn the anatomy and you can write a better prompt than any library, for any situation you'll ever face.

anatomy.purpose: Sets which expertise and judgment the AI borrows before it writes a single word.
anatomy.rule: Name a specific role with something at stake, not a job title. 'A recruiter who rejects vague resumes' beats 'a helpful assistant.'
anatomy.strong: You are a senior recruiter for remote ops roles who rejects any resume that buries results in duties.

anatomy.purpose: Gives the AI the raw material it needs. Without it, the AI invents facts to fill the gap.
anatomy.rule: Paste the actual source, the job post, your real experience, the client's email, never a summary of it from memory.
anatomy.weak: I have some experience in customer service.
anatomy.strong: Here is my resume: [PASTE FULL TEXT]. Here is the job post I'm targeting: [PASTE FULL TEXT].

anatomy.purpose: The single, concrete action you want performed, the verb that does the work.
anatomy.rule: One task, one verb, one object. Split anything with an 'and' in it into two prompts.
anatomy.strong: Rewrite my resume summary and top 3 bullets to match this specific job post.

anatomy.purpose: The boundaries that keep the output usable, length, tone limits, and what it must not do.
anatomy.rule: State limits as numbers and explicit rules, never adjectives. 'Under 150 words' beats 'concise.'
anatomy.strong: Under 120 words. No buzzwords like 'synergy' or 'passionate.' Don't invent metrics I didn't give you.

anatomy.purpose: The exact shape the output must take, so you can use it without reformatting it yourself.
anatomy.rule: Specify the structure directly, bullets, headers, a table, a script, not just 'organized.'
anatomy.strong: Output as 5 bullet points, each starting with a past-tense action verb, one line each.

anatomy.purpose: Shows the AI the pattern instead of describing it, the fastest way to close an ambiguity gap.
anatomy.rule: Paste one real example of the output you want, even a rough one, and say 'match this.'
anatomy.strong: Here's an email I sent last week that landed well: [PASTE]. Match this tone and sentence length.

anatomy.purpose: Keeps the output sounding like a person, the difference a reader feels in the first sentence.
anatomy.rule: Describe your actual voice with specifics, sentence length, formality, phrases you never say, not just 'friendly.'
anatomy.strong: Short sentences. No exclamation points. I say 'let's fix this,' not 'I would like to bring to your attention.'

anatomy.purpose: The rubric the AI should judge its own draft against before it ever reaches you.
anatomy.rule: Tell it what a good answer does that a bad one doesn't, then ask it to check its own draft against that before handing it over.
anatomy.strong: A good version names one specific result with a number in it. Check your draft against that rule before giving it to me.

principles.title: Specificity beats politeness
principles.desc: 'Please' and 'thank you' don't improve output. A precise noun does. Trade every 'nicely' for a number, a name, or a real example.

principles.title: Give it the rubric you'll judge by
principles.desc: Tell the AI what 'good' looks like before it drafts, not after you've read three bad drafts and are guessing why.

principles.title: Ask for options, not one answer
principles.desc: Request 3 versions and pick the strongest, or merge two. One draft is a guess dressed as an answer; three is an actual choice.

principles.title: Make it critique its own output
principles.desc: After it drafts, ask 'what's weak about this, and fix it.' AI catches its own generic phrasing better than you'd expect.

principles.title: Never trust a fact it produces
principles.desc: Names, numbers, dates, quotes, verify every one against a source you can point to. AI states wrong facts as confidently as right ones.

principles.title: Paste real material instead of describing it
principles.desc: Summarizing your resume from memory loses the exact details that make output specific. Paste the actual text, every time.

iterate.title: Draft
iterate.desc: Write your first version using every anatomy part you have real material for. Don't aim for perfect, aim for complete.

iterate.title: Run
iterate.desc: Send it. Read the whole output once before you judge any single line of it.

iterate.title: Diagnose
iterate.desc: Name exactly what's wrong using the signals below, 'this isn't it' isn't a diagnosis.

signals.symptom: Too generic, could apply to anyone
signals.cause: Missing Context, you described your situation instead of pasting it.
Missing Format, you never specified structure, length, or template.
Missing Voice, and it had no real sample of you to match.
Missing Constraints, you never told it what not to invent.

iterate.title: Change one thing
iterate.desc: Add or fix the single part you diagnosed as missing. Resist changing three things at once, you won't know which fix worked.

iterate.title: Re-run
iterate.desc: Send the revised prompt. Compare only the issue you targeted. Still off? Loop back to Diagnose.

critique.q: Does it contain a fact I can't verify?
critique.why: Names, numbers, claims, if you can't point to where it came from, it might be invented. Check before it goes out under your name.
Read it out loud. If you'd never say it that way, it reads as fake to the person on the other end too.

critique.q: Would I send this exactly as-is?
critique.why: If you're already planning to edit half of it, the prompt was missing something, go back to the loop instead of hand-fixing forever.

critique.q: Does it actually follow my constraints?
critique.why: AI drifts past word limits and sneaks in the words you banned. Check the numbers, not just the vibe.

critique.q: Is there a better version buried in a longer draft?
critique.why: Sometimes the third paragraph is the real opening line. Read the whole thing before you extract anything.

slopChecklist.tell: "In today's fast-paced world..." or any throat-clearing opener
slopChecklist.fix: Delete the first sentence. Almost every draft is stronger starting with the second one.

slopChecklist.tell: Padding three-item lists, 'reliable, efficient, and detail-oriented'
slopChecklist.fix: Cut two of the three. Keep only the one with a number attached to it.

slopChecklist.tell: Perfectly balanced sentences with no rough edges
slopChecklist.fix: Add the specific, slightly awkward detail a real person would actually say.

slopChecklist.tell: Em dashes doing the work a period should do
Words nobody says out loud, leverage, utilize, delve, robust, seamless
slopChecklist.fix: Swap for the plain verb: use, dig into, strong, works.

slopChecklist.tell: A closing line that just restates the opening, 'In conclusion...'
slopChecklist.fix: Delete it. If the piece needs a summary to be understood, the structure is the actual problem.

builder.intro: This quick builder covers the 6 core parts; Examples and Success criteria from the full anatomy above aren't included here. Fill in what you actually know. Skip what you don't have yet, the meter below will tell you exactly what that gap costs you.

fields.label: Role
fields.hint: Who should the AI be, and what's the stake if it gets this wrong?
fields.placeholder: e.g. A meticulous editor who rejects any sentence that could be shorter.

fields.label: Context
fields.hint: Paste your real material here, not a summary of it.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Paste the actual job post, email, or draft you're working from.

fields.label: Task
fields.hint: One verb, one object. What should it actually do?
fields.placeholder: e.g. Rewrite the second paragraph to lead with the result.

fields.label: Constraints
fields.placeholder: e.g. Under 150 words. No exclamation points. Don't invent numbers.

fields.label: Format
fields.hint: The exact shape you need back.
fields.placeholder: e.g. 3 bullet points, each under 15 words.

fields.label: Voice
fields.hint: How you actually sound, sentence length, what you never say.
fields.placeholder: e.g. Direct, short sentences, no corporate speak.

qualityLevels.label: Empty
qualityLevels.note: A prompt needs at least a Task before it can do anything.

qualityLevels.label: Bare
qualityLevels.note: This will produce something generic, it doesn't know your situation yet.

qualityLevels.label: Thin
qualityLevels.note: Still mostly guessing. Every gap gets filled with a generic assumption.

qualityLevels.label: Half-built
qualityLevels.note: Getting somewhere, but the parts you skipped are exactly where it turns generic.

qualityLevels.label: Workable
qualityLevels.note: Usable, but the gaps below will still produce generic output.

qualityLevels.label: Strong
qualityLevels.note: One gap left, usually the difference between output, and output that sounds like you.

qualityLevels.label: Complete
qualityLevels.note: All six parts filled. Copy it, run it, then diagnose whatever's still off.

useCases.title: Research
useCases.desc: Ask it to summarize a client's industry, a tool's docs, or a company before a call, then verify the two facts that matter most, yourself.

useCases.title: Drafting
useCases.desc: Get a fast first version of anything, an email, an SOP, a proposal, then edit it into your own voice before it goes out.

useCases.title: Critique
useCases.desc: Paste your own draft and ask it to find the weakest paragraph, the vaguest claim, or the line a client would push back on.

useCases.title: Mock interviews
useCases.desc: Have it play a skeptical hiring manager and grade your answers, practice handling pressure, not just reciting a script.

useCases.title: Learning a tool fast
useCases.desc: Ask it to explain the 20% of a tool's features that cover 80% of real jobs, then have it quiz you until you can do it cold.

useCases.title: Automation design
useCases.desc: Describe a repetitive task and ask it to map the trigger, the steps, and the edge cases, before you touch Zapier or Make.

specimensIntro: Four prompts pulled from an old copy-paste library, kept here only as specimens to dissect, not to paste. Read each for the pattern it uses, close the tab, then write your own version from the rule you found.

specimens.note: It never says 'be concise', it says 'quantify results' and 'mirror the exact keywords.' That's Constraints written as rules, not adjectives.
Format here is procedural, not a document shape, 'one question at a time, score after each answer.' Format can structure an interaction, not just a page.
'Definition of done' is Success criteria without naming it. Extract the rule it's using, don't copy the phrase.
'Suggest what to keep manual' is a Constraint framed as a scope boundary, not a word limit, a different flavor of the same part.
